extracted.intended_audience: federal government officials, legal counsel, and accounting/procurement officers handling appropriations and public funds
extracted.subtask_description: Legal/practical rules for the lawful use, timing, and disposition of United States appropriations (what may be charged to an appropriation, timing rules, transfers of property, donations, and related limitations). Intended to guide executive departments, accounting officers, and counsel in applying appropriation statutes and precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expenditures chargeable only to specifically provided appropriation
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the imperative rule that expenditures are payable out of the appropriation under which they are specifically provided for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applying this rule to an appropriation for construction/establishment (example: military telegraph line and meteorological station), expenses 'legitimately incurred in the construction' and in establishing the station are legally payable out of the appropriation and include mileage of the supervising officer, transportation of enlisted men, materials, hire of labor, erection of shelter, purchase of instruments, and every other expenditure necessary to carry out the act. (51 R. 666, Mar. 12, 1887.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimates as aid to construction of appropriation acts; limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Appropriations made in conformity with estimates imply authority to expend for articles designated in the estimates, but an appropriation act cannot be construed as appropriating for a certain article specified in the estimates unless the act either names that article or designates a class of objects within which it may reasonably be embraced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: appropriation that cut an estimate in half but did not mention 'observation towers' did not include the $35,000 item for towers; courts will not read a specific item from estimates into an appropriation unless the article is named or fairly and reasonably embraced in a designated class. (54 P. 112, June 14, 1892; 51 R. 666.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive/departmental discretion on necessity/cost subject to law
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions whether a particular expense is necessary or appropriate to the object for which an appropriation is made are generally within the discretion of the head of the department having control of disbursement, and that discretion is generally conclusive upon accounting officers and courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This discretion applies especially to necessity of an expenditure or the character/quality/reasonable cost of articles purchased, but it is a legal (not unlimited) discretion, subject to the terms of the appropriation and restrictions imposed by other laws; unconscionable transactions are not presumed. (United States v. Speed; Eamshaw v. United States; V Comp. Dec. 152; VIII Comp. Dec. 327.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative resolutions or authorizations without appropriation do not authorize spending
rubrics_metrics.description: A resolution directing an investigation or an act that provides for investigation but does not appropriate funds does not constitute a law making an appropriation for expenses of the investigation; expenses cannot be legally incurred from Treasury without an appropriation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Senate resolution May 2, 1900 directing Secretary of War to report on claims did not authorize him to involve the United States in expense of investigation. Similarly, an act authorizing a board and providing for report but not appropriating funds for improvement does not authorize the Secretary to proceed with the work himself. (C. 8199, May 5, 1900; C. 3721, Nov. 18, 1897.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Land purchases require explicit statutory authority (section 3736 R.S.)
rubrics_metrics.description: No land shall be purchased on account of the United States except under a law authorizing such purchase; an appropriation alone is not sufficient authority to purchase land.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: An appropriation for construction in vicinity of Manila was held not sufficient to justify purchase of land; acceptance of donation of lot in Alaska as site for telegraph office and quarters was not authorized. Supplemental statutory authority is required to acquire land. (C. 12154, Mar. 4, 1902; C. 21874, Feb. 18, 1908; C. 16898, Nov. 26, 1910.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriations must be applied solely to the object for which made (section 3678 R.S.)
rubrics_metrics.description: All sums appropriated for various branches of expenditure shall be applied solely to the object for which they are respectively made, and for no other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences/examples: funds for river and harbor improvements cannot be used to fence land intended for fortification; an appropriation for a designated road cannot be expended on an entirely different road; Army support or river/harbor funds cannot be expended to insure public property or employees; a 'Cavalry post' appropriation could not legally be used to construct a post for different 'mobile troops'. (C. 726, Jan. 8, 1895; C. 3635, Nov. 9, 1897; C. 23069, Mar. 16, 1909; C. 28948, Sept. 7, 1911.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Balances of annual appropriations — section 3690 R.S.: general rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Balances of appropriations made specifically for the service of a fiscal year and remaining unexpended at the end of that year shall only be applied to payment of expenses properly incurred during that year, or to fulfillment of contracts properly made within that year; balances not needed for such purposes shall be carried to the surplus fund.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rule does not apply to permanent or indefinite appropriations. Courts and accounting officers interpret this to mean: (1) supplies ordered and delivered within the year (or contracts made for delivery within the year) charge the appropriation, unless amount manifestly excessive; (2) contracts made within the fiscal year for deliveries within the year are chargeable even if deliveries occur after year end, subject to limitations; (3) contracts made within year with deliveries beginning that year and completed after expiration may be chargeable if replacements to reasonable stock on hand; (4) purchase of nonperishable articles needed for a fiscal year may be charged to that year's appropriation even if used over several years; (5) building contracts made and construction begun within the fiscal year may be chargeable though completed after expiration. (Section 3690; C. 8525, June 27, 1900; 22225, Oct. 18, 1907; 11 Comp. Dec. 454.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Permanent/indefinite appropriations exception and availability until expended
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 3690's limitations do not apply to appropriations known as permanent or indefinite; such appropriations remain available until expended (subject to completion of their object) and are not barred by the two-year lapse applicable to annual appropriations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: appropriation for enlargement of Governors Island (for permanent buildings) was considered permanent and available until expended; contingent permanent appropriations have been used years later when necessity still exists. However, if the object/ emergency that justified the appropriation no longer exists, the balance may be covered into the Treasury. (C. 14502, Apr. 20, 1903; G. 25291, July 16, 1909; G. 20718, Jan. 21, 1907.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and preparatory expenses: pre- and post-fiscal-year charges
rubrics_metrics.description: Necessary expenses connected with preparation of and entering into a contract payable from an annual appropriation may be paid from that appropriation when it becomes available, even if actually incurred prior to the fiscal year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: abstracts of title expenses incurred in June may be paid from appropriation available July 1; procurement actions like bids, guaranties, and acceptance may permit payment from the prior fiscal year's appropriation in some circumstances (e.g., mules accepted/delivered after close of fiscal year but with guaranty). Also, preliminary surveys, plans, and data collection needed to complete a project may be charged to the appropriation for erection/works. (C. 29072, Oct. 6, 1911; C. 26994, July 11, 1910; C. 16479, June 18, 1904; C. 8525.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Annual appropriation availability period (two-year rule) and lapse
rubrics_metrics.description: An appropriation made for a particular fiscal year is available for payment of proper charges against it incurred during that fiscal year for a period of two years after the expiration of the fiscal year; it then lapses and is no longer available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Army appropriations for a fiscal year had to be availed of and expended within two years from date of expiration to be used for repairs/reconstruction. (63 P., 337, Jan. 31, 1894; 49 P., 320, Oct. 3, 1891.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Transfers of departmental property: authority required unless no longer needed
rubrics_metrics.description: The Secretary of War (and analogous department heads) is not authorized, without authority of Congress, to turn over property of his department in his charge to another department for its use; but where the property is no longer needed for the purpose for which appropriated it may be transferred to another department without the consent of Congress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transfers are not treated as sales (title remains with the Government). Examples: instruments purchased from 'Medical and Hospital Supplies' could not be transferred to Agriculture; items no longer needed (e.g., condemned medical property) could be turned over to Forest Service; vessels have been transferred from Navy to War Department for use as transports when no longer needed by Navy. Applicable statutory/regulatory paragraphs (e.g., Par. 682, Par. 630 A.R. 1910) and precedent guide transfers. (C.1623, Aug. 7, 1895; C. 21850, July 26, 1907; C. 7840, Mar. 14, 1900.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Disposition of river and harbor property (statutory authority and crediting proceeds)
rubrics_metrics.description: The act of June 13, 1902 authorizes the disposition (sale or transfer) of property acquired for river and harbor improvements when no longer needed or serviceable, with proceeds from sale credited to the appropriation for the work for which it was purchased or to the project to/from which it is transferred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When river and harbor property is transferred to another project, the property is to be valued and credits/charges properly applied. Where no analogous statutory authority exists for other appropriations (e.g., District of Columbia), proceeds from disposition should be treated as 'Miscellaneous receipts' and deposited in the Treasury, with equitable apportionment where original funding was shared. Example: proposed exchange of machinery for a steamer—river and harbor appropriation chargeable only with difference in values; deposit treatment for District of Columbia share. (Act June 13, 1902; C. 27202, Aug. 30, 1910.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of private donations or offered funds to augment federal appropriations
rubrics_metrics.description: The Secretary (or executive department) lacks authority to permit construction or expend funds provided by private parties (donations) to carry out public works unless the consent of Congress to accept and expend the donation is obtained; contributions cannot be used to permit the department to exceed congressional appropriation limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a power company offering to furnish $10,000 for a river work in excess of appropriation could not legally have the Secretary let a contract or purchase in excess of appropriation; arrangement suggested where private party purchases and furnishes material or labor which officers could legally use, but direct expenditure beyond appropriation is not permitted. Similarly, Daughters of the American Revolution donation to build a post facility required Congress consent. (G. 1662, Aug. 23, 1895; O. 12344, Apr. 2, 1902.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific/special appropriation constrains permissible scope and amount
rubrics_metrics.description: When Congress makes a special appropriation for a certain object and amount, that appropriation expresses the amount legally expendable for that object; the appropriation cannot be lawfully expended to partially accomplish that object if completing the object would require additional appropriation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: appropriation for 'construction complete of a sewerage system' at Fort Monroe — statute contemplated completion within the appropriation and could not be used to construct a system whose completion required additional funds. Where a portion of the work can reasonably accomplish the object within appropriation (bringing road to 'fairly good condition'), limited flexibility may exist. (55 P. 364, Apr. 14, 1892; C. 3453, Aug. 24, 1897; Feb. 15, 1898.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriation deposits and quasi-public funds conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Money appropriated contingent on other sums or deposits (e.g., state or city appropriations or subscriptions) and deposited in subtreasury should be considered quasi-public money of the United States and remain on deposit until disbursed in conformity with the act of Congress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: funds appropriated for a monument contingent upon sums appropriated by New York State and City and subscriptions were deposited by Secretary of War and held as quasi-public funds to be disbursed according to the Congressional act. (G. 13999, Feb. 24, 1906.)
